Hi Arjun,

The warning indicates that the index in the model statement indicated is not a valid index. This could be caused by an index value being beyond the extent of valid indexing for a variable or by NAs as index values. It looks like the specific problem here is that you are creating the model without initializing `alive`, so the elements of `alive` are NA and hence the warning. It's not a problem per se, just a warning, but you can avoid the warning by initializing `alive` via `inits`.

Note that as suggested, `model$initializeInfo()` gives some potentially helpful information;

```
> sim_model$initializeInfo()
  [Note] Missing values (NAs) or non-finite values were found in model variables: phi, p, po, px, alive, mydata.
  [Note] This is not an error, but some or all variables may need to be initialized for certain algorithms to operate properly.
  [Note] For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).
```

-chris

Hi Arjun,

In addition to what Chris mentioned (set calculate = FALSE when building the model then the message would hopefully disappear), the nodes you specified for simulation are not quite right. More specifically, you should simulate for nodes that are dependencies (excluding self) of the top-level parameters phi and p if you want to set true values for phi and p:
  # Get nodes for simulation
  sim_nodes <- sim_model$getDependencies(c("phi", "p"), self = FALSE)
Otherwise you can generate true values for them as well. Also, z is not a node in your code, but you specified initial values for it. I guess it is a typo, and just use alive instead:
# Initialize the initial state for each individual
  initial_states <- sample(1:2, N, replace = TRUE)
  sim_model$alive[,1] <- initial_states
But I do not see why you need to simulate initial states in a CJS model. IMO, just set alive[i, 1] <- 1 in your model code instead of using dcat. 

Something not quite relevant, you can directly use the custom distributions (e.g. dCJS) in package nimbleEcology for many common ecological models. 

Best wishes,
Wei

Hi Arjun, sorry, my initial response was a more generic response about understanding missing dynamic indexes.

In your simulation case, if you want to set top-level parameters and then simulate all the way down through the model you'll need
getDependencies(c("p", "phi"), self = FALSE, downstream = TRUE)

That should allow you to do the simulation you want. As Wei said, if you want to avoid seeing the warnings when you create the model, you can pass `calculate=FALSE` to the `nimbleModel` call.

As a side note, it works ok as you have it, but using a list `f` and the variable `s` in your model code that come from the global environment is not encouraged. It's best to pass everything needed for the indexing of the for loops in via `constants`, and you would need to avoid the use of lists as components of the `constants` list. So you could pass in something like `constants = list(N = N, nyears = nyears, f = f[[s]])` and then use `f[i]` in your code instead of `f[[s]][i]`.

-chris

I think you need to turn on 'calculate = TRUE'  when building the model or run 'sim_model$calculate()' before you simulate data to make sure you can actually generate data by simulation. I would say this is not a big deal here, nothing to worry about. I do not see a neat way to handle this, but other people may have some good ideas.

Hi Arjun, sorry, my initial response was a more generic response about understanding missing dynamic indexes.

In your simulation case, if you want to set top-level parameters and then simulate all the way down through the model you'll need
getDependencies(c("p", "phi"), self = FALSE, downstream = TRUE)

That should allow you to do the simulation you want. As Wei said, if you want to avoid seeing the warnings when you create the model, you can pass `calculate=FALSE` to the `nimbleModel` call.

As a side note, it works ok as you have it, but using a list `f` and the variable `s` in your model code that come from the global environment is not encouraged. It's best to pass everything needed for the indexing of the for loops in via `constants`, and you would need to avoid the use of lists as components of the `constants` list. So you could pass in something like `constants = list(N = N, nyears = nyears, f = f[[s]])` and then use `f[i]` in your code instead of `f[[s]][i]`.
